Lucie County could become a data center, according to a rezoning application sent to the city of Fort Pierce.Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center.WATCH BELOW: New 203-acre data center proposed in St. Lucie CountyThe rezoning application said, "the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial."Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area."You have a beautiful view all the time," Whiteside said.When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate."I hate that idea," Whiteside said.The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project."He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said.Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power & Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system.According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food."Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions."Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said.Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution."If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said.The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. According to the application, "the partner company would need to submit to the City a site plan application for the proposed data center and obtain City approval of the site plan."The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board on Sept.

Lucie Police Department is announcing an operational pause on the use of all Automated License Plate Reader technology, widely recognized as Flock cameras, according to a press release from the Port St. PSLPD’s announcement comes in light of FDOT’s memorandum regarding the revoking of permits for ALPR systems on state roads. During the pause, PSLPD says that ALPR access will be limited exclusively to exigent circumstances regarding immediate threat to human life, or in circumstances in which access to ALPR information may help prevent the loss of life or threat to great bodily harm. Police Chief Leo Niemczyk weighed in on the decision to remove pause the use of ALPR technology. See also: Motorcycle crash shuts down I-95 Southbound in Martin County This is a dedicated balance. On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes, he said. On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability, and public safety. We are committed to finding that balance and doing what is right for the people we serve. PSLPD says it will continue to monitor developments at the state level and review any additional guidance as it becomes available.

A packed crowd filled Village Hall Tuesday night as residents urged leaders to hit the pause button on future hyperscale data center projects . But by the end of the meeting, the debate over data centers had led to a major shakeup in village leadership. After hours of public comment, the Indiantown Village Council voted 4-1 against a proposed resolution that would have temporarily paused new large-scale data center applications while the village drafted regulations addressing infrastructure, utilities and community impacts. Council members said they want new legal counsel to review the proposal and help craft language that can withstand legal scrutiny before bringing it back for consideration. Shortly after that vote, the council voted to terminate Village Manager Taryn Kryzda, who had served the village since 2024, effective immediately. The council also voted to remove Village Attorney Wade Vose from the meeting and move forward with obtaining interim legal counsel. Vose had previously submitted his resignation, but council members voted to end his participation in the meeting and proceed in a different direction. Late Tuesday night, the council appointed Michael Giardino as interim village manager. Giardino recently served as Stuart's city manager before being fired by the Stuart City Commission last week. Council members said the leadership changes reflect a desire to move the village in a new direction as it tackles major issues, including future data center development. As she left Village Hall, Kryzda offered a brief response to CBS12 News. "I'm happy to go home early." Before the vote, residents spent hours voicing concerns about the potential impact multiple hyperscale data centers could have on the community. Some residents created a website featuring an interactive map highlighting several proposed projects across the area. Penny Kaminsky-Preli used the map to point out some of those developments. "This is Project Growler, another 600,000 hyperscale data center. Another one in the application." Others worried about how close future projects could be to schools, parks and neighborhoods. "I'm not against them coming to the village. I'm more concerned with their proximity to things like the school or field elementary school. I'm more concerned with the proximity to Booker Park," resident Eric Miller said. Former Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback urged council members to use what he described as authority recently granted to local governments by state lawmakers. "There have been 19 moratoriums that have been passed in Florida this year. Not a single one of them have been challenged by a data center plaintiff," Fishback said. Village leaders told CBS12 News they expect to have interim legal counsel in place soon and hope to bring a revised data center resolution back before the council within the next week or two.

The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, and Treasure Coast law enforcement is responding to the decision.FDOT sent the memorandum on Monday, which came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology "out of control" last week.WATCH BELOW: Florida orders license plate reader removal; Treasure Coast reactsNot everyone disagrees with the move. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras."I think it's an invasion of privacy," Reilly said. "I'm personally not a fan."But others in the community see the technology as a critical safety tool.Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe."I think it's super important to have that kind of technology out there to catch the bad guys," Bailey said.Neighbor Kristina Ramsey pointed to the cameras' track record."I definitely think it's helped catch a lot of criminals," Kristina said.Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the license plate readers, like Flock cameras, after they aided in a homicide arrest last month."We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said.On Tuesday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek responded directly to the state's removal decision."What's that do to the Martin County citizens? It makes us fundamentally less safe," Budensiek said.Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras."We stopped and arrested President (Donald) Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew," Budensiek said.Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said legislation, not removal, is the right path forward."Without those cameras out there on US-1, it's a needle in a haystack," Snyder said.Snyder called for a measured approach to address privacy concerns while preserving the public safety benefits."Meaningful legislation that regulates their use, protects privacy, but somehow allows us to keep the cameras and keep the community safe," Snyder said.Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record."If people still don't trust law enforcement, I would be OK with, and I believe the Florida sheriffs would be OK with, a public professional auditing system," Budensiek said.WPTV learned Tuesday that Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. We're also learning on Tuesday, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will be limiting license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie Police Department has significantly limited the use of automated license plate reader technology after the Florida Department of Transportation issued a directive to remove certain cameras from state highway rights-of-way. 31, 2026, FDOT issued a memorandum revoking permits for license plate reader technology systems located within state highway rights-of-way and requiring affected equipment to be removed within 30 days. The PSLPD has seven cameras within FDOT rights-of-way that will be removed to comply with the directive. Effective immediately, the department is placing an operational pause on the use of its remaining automated license plate reader technology. Access to automated license plate reader technology systems during this pause will be limited to exigent circumstances involving an immediate threat to human life, such as cases involving a missing or endangered child, an endangered vulnerable adult, a homicide investigation with an immediate threat, or other situations where automated license plate reader technology information could prevent loss of life or great bodily harm. Every request to access automated license plate reader technology during the pause will require prior approval and authorization from Chief Leo Niemczyk. The PSLPD highlighted the effectiveness of automated license plate reader technology as an investigative tool, noting its role in locating missing people, recovering stolen vehicles, identifying suspects, developing leads and solving crimes. Since 2022, auto burglaries in Port St. Lucie have decreased by 17%, with automated license plate reader technology providing investigators an additional resource to protect the community. “This is a delicate balance. On one hand, we have a technology that has proven to be an important tool for our officers and investigators and has helped us protect people and solve crimes. On the other, we have a responsibility to listen to our community, respect the direction of our state leaders, and ensure our policies reflect the highest standards of trust, accountability and public safety. We are committed to finding that balance and doing what is right for the people we serve,” said Niemczyk. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro also sent out a press release on Tuesday updating their policy on the use of Automatic License Plate Reader Technology. Use of the technology will now require prior approval from the undersheriff and be limited to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered person investigations. Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods' attorney, Douglas Duncan , filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m. 2, before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea. The development marks a change from Woods' previous position in the case. In March , the 50-year-old golf legend entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. It is not yet clear from the newly filed notice what plea Woods intends to enter Wednesday or whether the hearing is part of a negotiated plea agreement. See also: ' Rolling prison’: 2 women accused of heinous sexual abuse, neglect of 4 children The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket, according to the arrest affidavit. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.

The Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) ordered local agencies to remove license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, and Treasure Coast law enforcement is responding to the decision.FDOT sent the memorandum on Monday, which came after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology "out of control" last week.WATCH BELOW: Florida orders license plate reader removal; Treasure Coast reactsNot everyone disagrees with the move. Stuart resident Sean Reilly said he has never supported the cameras."I think it's an invasion of privacy," Reilly said. "I'm personally not a fan."But others in the community see the technology as a critical safety tool.Neighbor Brandee Bailey said license plate readers play an important role in keeping the community safe."I think it's super important to have that kind of technology out there to catch the bad guys," Bailey said.Neighbor Kristina Ramsey pointed to the cameras' track record."I definitely think it's helped catch a lot of criminals," Kristina said.Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the license plate readers, like Flock cameras, after they aided in a homicide arrest last month."We got a murderer behind bars because of this. We got this guy off the streets because of the Flock system," Flowers said.On Tuesday, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek responded directly to the state's removal decision."What's that do to the Martin County citizens? It makes us fundamentally less safe," Budensiek said.Budensiek pointed to several major arrests made with the help of the cameras."We stopped and arrested President (Donald) Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew," Budensiek said.Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said legislation, not removal, is the right path forward."Without those cameras out there on US-1, it's a needle in a haystack," Snyder said.Snyder called for a measured approach to address privacy concerns while preserving the public safety benefits."Meaningful legislation that regulates their use, protects privacy, but somehow allows us to keep the cameras and keep the community safe," Snyder said.Budensiek proposed limiting camera use to criminal investigations and missing persons cases, requiring a case number and report for public record."If people still don't trust law enforcement, I would be OK with, and I believe the Florida sheriffs would be OK with, a public professional auditing system," Budensiek said.WPTV learned Tuesday that Port St. Lucie police is pausing the use of license plate readers in the city. We're also learning on Tuesday, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office will be limiting license plate reader use to investigations involving forcible felonies and missing or endangered persons.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County could become a data center, according to a rezoning application sent to the city of Fort Pierce. Willow Lakes LLC, the owner of 203 acres of land off West Midway Road and Interstate 95, submitted a rezoning application in June to change 174 acres to light industrial use to allow for a data center. WATCH BELOW: New 203-acre data center proposed in St. Lucie County The rezoning application said, "the applicant intends to develop a data center on the portion of the property to be zoned Light Industrial." Parker Whiteside, who lives about a mile and a half from the property, said she values the quiet, open character of the area. "You have a beautiful view all the time," Whiteside said. When asked about the potential data center, her reaction was immediate. "I hate that idea," Whiteside said. The land was originally planned for the Koa Bay Surf Park Community, with developer Devcon Enterprises. Attorney Lee Dobbins, who represents Willow Lakes LLC, said those plans fell through after the property owner could not raise sufficient capital for the project. "He was looking at what else he could potentially do at the property," Dobbins said. Dobbins said the landowner believes the property is well-suited for a data center, citing existing Florida Power Light transmission lines on the site and a man-made lake that could be used for a closed-loop cooling system. According to the rezoning application, the applicant requests the remaining 26 acres to be zoned general commercial, "intended for development for commercial retail uses, and could include a hotel, gas station and/or restaurants/fast food." Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick said the proposal could be an appropriate use of the land, but he has conditions. "Data centers are kind of the rage right now," Broderick said. Broderick said he wants developers to demonstrate there will be no impact to groundwater, no impacts to user fees from power consumption and no noise pollution. "If they don't, then I will not be supportive of it," Broderick said. The rezoning application said that if rezoning is approved, the applicant intends to enter into an agreement with a partner company which would develop the data center. According to the application, "the partner company would need to submit to the City a site plan application for the proposed data center and obtain City approval of the site plan." The application is scheduled to go before the Planning and Zoning Board on Sept.

Lucie homeowners are finding a flyer in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro , the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. According to the city's proposal, about 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit. One resident recounted her first reaction to getting the letter. I thought it was going to be money, not on my taxes, said Deborah Koon-Martin, a PSL homeowner. That difference is the part homeowners are most likely to notice when the notice arrives. Not every property qualifies for the larger amount. The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping, Koon-Martin said. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested with gun at private school, police say When Koon-Martin was asked what she wanted from the city, her answer was clear. Because it makes it better. You have maggots crawling out of the trash. I’d rather go back to twice a week, said Koon-Martin. Council members also agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. "It's the taxpayers' money. The taxpayers were the ones who were wronged," Councilman Anthony Bonna said. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

Ed Markey of Massachusetts secured the Democratic nomination in his bid for a third term in office Tuesday, fighting off a challenger who argued that it was time for a generational change.Markey, 80, defeated U.S. Seth Moulton, 47, in the Senate primary.Moulton told voters it was time to do away with the “status quo.” Markey pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it was Moulton — not the older incumbent — who was out of touch with the state’s voters.Markey has boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs.In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle.Markey has been a fixture in Massachusetts politics since the 1970s and is seeking a third six-year term. Moulton, 47, repeatedly argued on the campaign trail that the Democratic Party is stuck in the “status quo” and questioned Markey’s accomplishments during his lengthy time in office.“People ought to ask, what are you going to accomplish in the next six years that you haven’t been able to accomplish in the last 50?” Moulton said.Markey pointed to Moulton’s more moderate positions to argue that it is Moulton — not the older incumbent — who is out of touch with Massachusetts voters. Markey boasted about his 2022 climate bill and called for an end to the war in Iran to bring down energy costs.He also sharply criticized Moulton for opposing “Medicare for All” — though Moulton has called for universal healthcare.“He has a backwards-looking political agenda,” Markey said.In heavily Democratic Massachusetts, the primary is considered the most critical election hurdle, and the winner is expected to prevail in the general election in November.The Senate race was not the only generational challenge for Democrats on Tuesday's ballot. A similar dynamic played out in the 8th Congressional District, where Patrick Roath hoped to oust longtime incumbent Rep. Stephen Lynch, and in the 1st Congressional District of western Massachusetts, where progressive public school teacher Jeromie Whalen faced against Rep. Richard Neal.RELATED NEWS | 'Too late' for Trump to make major changes to how mail-in voting works, expert saysMoulton's comments on transgender children have been an issueDuring the campaign Markey repeatedly pointed out that Moulton, in 2024, raised eyebrows among some in the party for saying he did not want his daughters playing sports against transgender girls.Critics said he was echoing President Donald Trump’s talking points against allowing transgender athletes in girls’ and women’s sports.Moulton has since apologized for his remarks, saying it was not his intention to hurt the transgender community and stressing his support for other transgender rights bills.“If you’re in the trans community or you’re a trans kid feeling the weight of the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, you matter,” Moulton said during an August debate. “You’re valued, and I will always have your back.”Moulton, who enlisted in the Marines after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, and served four tours of duty in Iraq, was first elected to Massachusetts’ 6th Congressional District in 2014. He launched a 2020 presidential campaign but dropped it after a few months.Markey was elected to the Senate in 2013. Before that he represented Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District from 1976 to 2013.Markey notably fended off a challenge in 2020 from Rep. Joe Kennedy III, a younger rival from one of the nation's most famous political families. Markey did so by aligning himself with the liberal wing of the Democratic Party.Antoine Hilaire, a 76-year-old Democrat who voted for Markey in Brockton on Tuesday, said being older can be a positive because it offers people experience and wisdom.“If the older one is doing the better job, I don’t know,” he said. It’s not a big, big, big problem.”Longtime Democratic House incumbents also face younger challengersLynch, 71, has held the 8th District seat in south Boston since 2001. He faced Roath, a 39-year-old lawyer who contended that it is time to end “wait-your-turn” politics. Lynch stressed the value of experience inside Congress.Lynch has fended off other youth challenges in the past, but Roath’s campaign hoped for a boost of excitement after longtime Democratic incumbent U.S. John Larson was defeated by former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin in August in neighboring Connecticut. Like Roath, Bronin called for the need for generational change while running against an establishment politician.Meanwhile the 1st District primary in western Massachusetts pitted Neal, 77, against Whalen, 39.Neal, known as the dean of the New England House delegation, was first elected in 1988. Whalen ran to the left of Neal, calling for Medicare for All and questioning whether Neal has done enough to oppose Trump’s agenda.Whalen recently was endorsed by Our Revolution, a progressive organization founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

The Town of Jupiter is set to launch its first-ever municipal fire department on Oct. 1, ushering in a new era of public safety that connects back to a 70-year history of local service. The new Jupiter Fire Rescue agency will take over service from Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, with many of its new firefighters having deep roots in the community they will now protect.WATCH: Jupiter's new municipal fire department prepares for Oct. 1 launchWith the transition just one month away, the new department marks a significant shift in emergency services for the town's residents and a return to a dedicated, Jupiter-focused fire service for the first time in nearly four decades.While this is the town's first government-run fire department, the history of firefighting in Jupiter began with volunteers more than 70 years ago."Back in 1950, we had a new chamber of commerce for Jupiter, and they realized one of the things that the community needed, as it was starting to grow post-World War II, is it needs some fire support," a local historian named Josh explained.That first department was a world away from modern fire rescue. It consisted of volunteers with no official uniforms, using converted military trucks and hand sprayers to protect their growing community. In 1985, these services were merged into the larger Palm Beach County Fire Rescue system.The new Jupiter Fire Rescue department is reviving the tradition of locals serving their own community. The department recently held a push-in ceremony for its first new fire engine and swore in its inaugural class of firefighters."Twenty-nine people that have joined Jupiter Fire Rescue are local hometown Jupiter people… and they have come home to serve their community," Fire Chief Darrel Donatto said.As they prepare for the official launch, the new crews are undergoing intensive training. Their preparation has also included learning more about the community's history, including a recent visit to the Jupiter Inlet Lighthouse, according to the historian.On Oct. 1, the new department will begin writing the next chapter of Jupiter's history, responding to calls from its new fire station and reviving a long-standing legacy of community-based service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. What began as a hit-and-run investigation in Palm City turned into a massive multi-agency manhunt Wednesday, ending with deputies pulling a suspect from a swamp along the Martin-St. CBS12 News was there as deputies emerged from the water with 39-year-old Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce in handcuffs. Both Daceus and the deputies who tracked him down were drenched from the murky swamp water after an hours-long search. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Daceus was wanted in connection with a hit-and-run crash in Palm City. Investigators say he fled the scene and ran through the Windstone community off Southwest Rivers End Way before disappearing into a large swampy area near the county line. His disappearance sparked a large-scale search involving Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies, K-9 teams, aviation units, drone operators, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission officers, and Port St. The search lasted more than two hours as helicopters circled overhead and officers established a perimeter around nearby neighborhoods. See also: One red-light camera ticket led to suspended license, criminal citation for PBC man "It's not an everyday occurrence," nearby resident and State Rep. Toby Overdorf told CBS12 News. The significant law enforcement presence forced the closure of parts of Southwest Murphy Road and temporarily prevented some residents from returning home. "With that kind of police presence, we felt we were okay," Overdorf said. The sheriff's office says the coordinated effort ultimately paid off, with technology playing a key role in locating Daceus. Court records reviewed Wednesday show Daceus previously had only a handful of traffic-related violations in Indian River County, including driving with a suspended license. Now, investigators say he could be facing far more serious charges. Despite the unusual scene unfolding near their homes, residents say they never doubted deputies would find the suspect. Martin County always gets their guy," Overdorf said. Daceus was being booked into the Martin County Jail Wednesday evening. Investigators are continuing to review the case and determine what charges he will ultimately face.

Two parked trucks were heavily damaged in a violent crash in Port St. Security video recorded the crash, which shows a black truck traveling at a high rate of speed on SW Lucero Drive around 3:40 p.m. The truck goes off the road into the grass and then slams into the two parked trucks. "When I heard the crash, I thought it was thunder," Elaine Harmon, a neighbor, said. "I heard a loud explosion," said another neighbor, Rocky Burkhead. "Thought it was just lightning like we've been having over the last few days." But when Burkhead stepped outside, he realized the situation was far worse than a weather-related incident. "I had no idea what to think. I was just at a loss for words. My first concern was, 'Is he OK?'" Burkhead said. Lucie police said the man in the black truck sustained only minor injuries. However, Burkhead said the damage to the two parked trucks hit in the collision was extensive. Both trucks belong to Burkhead and are essential for his pressure washing business. I had to rent a U-Haul today. You're limited on what you can do, how far you can go," Burkhead said. Neighbors said the crash is the most dramatic example of speeding on Southwest Lucero Drive but emphasized it is not an isolated incident. The speed limit on the road is 25 mph, but residents said drivers rarely adhere to it. "People do fly by on this road all the time," Courtney Gray, a neighbor, said. "There's a big problem with speeding on this road," Burkhead said. Residents are particularly concerned because the road lacks sidewalks, yet many people walk along it with children and pets. "I walk every day with (my baby) in the stroller or whatever. I'm just so thankful we weren't home when it happened," Gray said. "I think what they need to do is put some officers in the area, pull a few people over with some heavy-duty fines," Burkhead said. "Seems like something like this is going to keep happening if we don't have speed bumps," Gray said. Lucie police have not yet responded to inquiries about arrests related to the crash or the possibility of speed bumps or additional patrols. Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after firefighters quickly contained the blaze, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The fire was reported just after 6:30 a.m. in the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane. When crews arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage of the home. According to the homeowner, a lithium-ion battery had been charging in the garage before the fire started. Firefighters immediately evacuated the residence and worked to contain the flames, preventing the fire from spreading beyond the garage. Officials said crews successfully extinguished the fire, and no neighboring structures were threatened. Fire rescue officials called the incident a close call and are reminding residents to follow proper lithium-ion battery safety practices. They encourage people to unplug batteries once they are fully charged to help prevent overheating and potential fires. Teacher pay negotiations are officially underway in Palm Beach County, but this year's talks come with an added challenge: another significant drop in student enrollment that could further strain district finances.Last year, educators and supporters pushed through a tight budget to secure a 3.5% raise for teachers.WATCH BELOW: Teacher pay talks begin amid 7,000-student enrollment dropThis year, negotiations are beginning as the School District of Palm Beach County grapples with the loss of nearly 7,000 students and the funding reductions that come with it.The district and the Classroom Teachers Association, commonly known as the CTA, have already held their first bargaining session."What we're negotiating at this point is what is it that every single teacher needs to have in order to continue to be able to pay their bills where they live and continue to work in the schools that they've chosen to serve," said Classroom Teachers Association President Gordan Longhofer.While teacher contracts are negotiated every year, Longhofer said each round of talks brings a different set of circumstances.This year's challenge centers around enrollment. According to district figures, K-12 enrollment declined by 6,959 students, including losses at both district-operated and charter schools. Fewer students translate into less state funding, creating additional pressure on the budget."We understand that is problematic," Longhofer said.Last school year, negotiations came to an impasse over teacher salaries because of funding and the push for raises.This lasted nearly a year before School Board members voted to give teachers a 3.5% raise.Still, Longhofer remains optimistic that an agreement can be reached without the prolonged negotiations seen in some previous years.When asked what he would say to teachers concerned about the district's financial outlook, Longhofer responded, "I don't necessarily believe we can't get to a deal in more typical time frame."Before the start of the school year, Superintendent Mike Burke projected a much smaller decline in enrollment."Our best forecast is that we'll be down about 2,900 this year," Burke said.The actual number came in at more than double that estimate.Despite declining enrollment trends seen across Florida, Burke said the district is not considering closing schools.When asked whether Palm Beach County could face school closures like other districts, Burke responded, "No, we're trying to utilize our resources; we've been able to avoid that. We've actually opened some new schools because in Palm Beach County we still have parts of the county that are growing rapidly."Instead, the district plans to shift teachers and staff where they are needed most and is implementing a hiring freeze to help offset funding losses tied to state enrollment formulas."We need better funding," Burke said.Teacher pay conversations this year are also unfolding as Palm Beach County voters prepare to decide the future of the district's 1-mill property tax referendum in November. District leaders say the referendum generates more than $200 million annually for schools. Approximately half of that funding supports teacher salaries, while the remainder helps pay for choice programs, mental health resources and school security.It's been approved by voters during the last two elections.For many educators, the referendum money has become a critical part of their compensation."This money really helps teachers tremendously," said Alicia Carr, a teacher at Jupiter Elementary School.Carr has worked in education for 14 years, including the last six years at Jupiter Elementary.Like many teachers, she says the issue goes beyond numbers on a paycheck."No one goes into teaching for the money, but you want to be able to live," Carr said.Under the referendum, teachers receive additional compensation based on their years of experience:$1,000 after their first year$5,000 for teachers with five to nine years of experience$10,000 for teachers with 10 or more years in the classroomCarr said losing that supplemental pay would have a major impact on educators across the district."Even with our raise it's still a struggle so losing this $10,000 would be astronomical for many people," Carr said.The teachers union says only one negotiating session has taken place so far, and discussions remain in the early stages.Both sides are now working toward an Oct. 1 deadline to reach an agreement on teacher raises.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. By: Samantha Roesler Posted JENSEN BEACH, Fla. — Two people and a dog are safe Monday morning after a garage fire in Jensen Beach that firefighters believe was caused by a charging lithium-ion battery. Martin County Fire Rescue and Stuart Fire Rescue crews responded to the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane just after 6:30 a.m., where they found heavy smoke coming from a garage. The homeowner told firefighters they had been charging a lithium-ion battery in the garage when the fire started. Firefighters extinguished the fire before it could spread to other structures. Lithium-ion batteries are commonly found in smartphones, laptops, e-bikes, scooters, and many other electronic devices. While generally safe when used properly, they can pose fire risks if damaged, overcharged, or exposed to extreme temperatures. The National Fire Prevention Association provides additional safety guidelines for lithium-ion battery use on their website.

Lucie homeowners are finding a flyer in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bill. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro , the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial. In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties. According to the city's proposal, about 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit. One resident recounted her first reaction to getting the letter. I thought it was going to be money, not on my taxes, said Deborah Koon-Martin, a PSL homeowner. That difference is the part homeowners are most likely to notice when the notice arrives. Not every property qualifies for the larger amount. The decision to issue credits instead of checks drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. You can use the money for other things. You're going to pay your taxes anyway, so it's not really helping, Koon-Martin said. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience. See also: West Palm Beach man arrested with gun at private school, police say When Koon-Martin was asked what she wanted from the city, her answer was clear. Because it makes it better. You have maggots crawling out of the trash. I’d rather go back to twice a week, said Koon-Martin. Council members also agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. "It's the taxpayers' money. The taxpayers were the ones who were wronged," Councilman Anthony Bonna said. The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Residents have continued pressing the city over once-a-week pickup, and the council considered whether settlement money could pay for a second weekly collection day before rejecting that option, saying it would only work until the money ran out. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said his agency will comply with Florida’s order to remove license plate readers from state roadways but will keep cameras not covered by the directive in place as he seeks statewide privacy safeguards. In a video statement, Budensiek said the Martin County Sheriff’s Office has used license plate readers successfully, appropriately, and legally for the past decade to identify traveling criminals. He said the cameras have helped deputies stop kidnapping suspects, burglary crews, human traffickers, gun traffickers and drug traffickers. Budensiek also said the technology helped authorities stop a man accused of plotting to assassinate President Donald Trump . The Florida Department of Transportation has given agencies 30 days to remove Flock cameras and similar license plate reader technology from state roads and revoked previously approved permits. The order does not apply to cameras located off state rights of way. Budensiek said the sheriff’s office will follow the directive but argued the removal makes Martin County fundamentally less safe. The license plate readers that are not affected by this order will remain in place until we get solidified, thoughtful legislation in place that helps us keep the citizens of Martin County safe, Budensiek said. Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw also said the technology should come with protections against misuse. In a statement to CBS12 News, Bradshaw called automated license plate readers indispensable to law enforcement and said they have led to significant arrests of dangerous suspects. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has also strongly defended the technology. In recent comments to CBS12 News, Flowers pointed to the use of license plate readers in the investigation into the killing of Vero Beach hairdresser Dawn Kriskewic. Investigators used the cameras to track suspect Matthew Waggle’s movements after he fled Florida; he was later captured in West Virginia. So for everybody who wants to talk about how bad this system is, we got a murderer behind bars because of this, Flowers said. Flowers noted that Flock is one company that provides automated license plate readers, but said the wider debate involves the use of the technology itself. We say Flock, but it’s license plate readers, because they’re just one brand. It’s all license plate readers, Flowers said. He also argued that the technology can help clear people who are wrongly suspected of crimes. If we’re able to show that that person’s vehicle was nowhere near the homicide, Flowers said, that’s a great way for us to show that somebody is innocent as well. Budensiek said he understands privacy concerns and has proposed legislation to local state lawmakers and the Florida Sheriffs Association. His proposal would limit license plate reader searches to criminal investigations and missing-person cases and require a case number, report and supervisory approval. The proposal also calls for internal and external audits, short data-retention periods and a prohibition on private companies possessing or selling the data. Budensiek said he would support having the Florida Department of Law Enforcement or an independent professional auditor review the systems. Complete elimination of this program will result in a payday and a holiday for the traveling criminals who have plagued this county and all of South Florida, Budensiek said. Read the full transcript of Sheriff Budensiek's video below: "I'm Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek and I want to speak directly to the citizens of Martin County. For this conversation, context matters. For the past 10 years, the Martin County Sheriff's Office has successfully, appropriately, and legally used license plate readers to protect the citizens of Martin County against the traveling criminals. "To highlight some of those cases, we stopped and arrested President Trump's would-be assassin. Last year, we stopped a kidnapper with two of our young girls headed to Nebraska. We stopped a traveling rooftop burglary crew. We've stopped human traffickers, gun traffickers, drug traffickers, and the list goes on. Recently, the Florida Department of Transportation ordered the removal of all license plate readers or such devices from their rideways. "Well, what's that do to the Martin County citizens? It makes us fundamentally less safe. So the question is, what are you going to do, sheriff, with these license plate readers? Well, first and foremost, of course, we're going to comply with the order. But the license plate readers that are not affected by this order will remain in place until we get solidified, thoughtful legislation in place that helps us keep the citizens of Martin County safe. "Prior to this order, I've talked to many citizens in Martin County. I've read the news reports. I believe all sides of the argument. We've got to protect the privacy of our citizens while protecting our citizens. And that's a very difficult balancing act. As part of that though, I've reached out and proposed legislation to our local state representative and to the Florida Sheriff's Association. "And the legislation is as follows. License plate readers can only be used for criminal investigations or missing persons. Has to have a case number and a report attached. So, you create a public record that the public can come in and see what you've done with your license plate readers. It has to have supervisory approval. "It has to have an internal auditing system. It has to have an external auditing system. And I would suggest the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. And on top of that, if people still don't trust law enforcement, I would be okay with, and I believe the Florida Sheriff's would be okay with a public professional auditing system. "There has to be a short retention period. You can't keep this information forever. And I think of most importance to a lot of our individuals, this data cannot be in the hands of a private industry who sells our information. Complete elimination of this program will result in a payday and a holiday for the traveling criminals who have plagued this county and all of South Florida. "In closing, I want you, the citizens of Martin County, to know that I'll do everything possible, leverage every resource, every asset that I have legally available to keep you, the citizens of Martin County, safe."

A controversial policing tactic that permitted staggering amounts of deadly fentanyl to reach the streets as federal authorities sought to build bigger drug cases is now under investigation by Republicans on the House Oversight Committee.The committee's chairman, Rep. James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky, sent a letter Monday to Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting records related to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration's controversial strategy of monitoring — yet not seizing — major fentanyl shipments.The request echoes concerns raised by officials in New Mexico, the epicenter of the fentanyl crisis, where DEA whistleblowers recently reported being ordered to stand down rather than seize hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills in possible violation of Justice Department rules intended to safeguard communities. Last week, the state's attorney general, Raúl Torrez, sued the Justice Department seeking to force it to turn over some of the same records being sought by Republicans on Comer's committee."While DEA agents may not have the resources to intercept every single known shipment, a policy directing them not to intercept significant shipments is unconscionable and undoubtedly resulted in considerable harm and lives lost," Comer wrote in the letter, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press.The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The lawsuit and congressional inquiry come two months after an AP investigation found DEA agents repeatedly monitored major fentanyl shipments in New Mexico between 2023 and 2025 that were allowed to hit the streets as federal authorities built out criminal cases.The fentanyl went unseized amid the deadliest drug epidemic in U.S. history and even as DEA led a public awareness campaign — "One Pill Can Kill" — emphasizing that even a few milligrams of the substance can be lethal. Last year, the White House designated the synthetic opioid a "weapon of mass destruction."Comer requested records covering only the Biden administration, citing what he described as its "relaxation of fentanyl risk mitigation protocols" developed during President Donald Trump's first term. The protocols, Comer said, should have prevented the fentanyl from hitting the streets in such large numbers.The earlier policy, adopted in 2017, called on agents to "seize or otherwise prevent the distribution" of fentanyl "as soon as practicable." The department rewrote those rules in 2024 to afford law enforcement far more discretion in whether to take action to prevent fentanyl trafficking, citing "the benefits to be achieved through preserving the investigation."AP reporting found the investigative strategy — known as allowing drugs to "walk" — continued into Trump's second administration during the run-up to the largest fentanyl bust in DEA history, a takedown announced in May 2025 by then-Attorney General Pam Bondi.As part of that investigation, authorities seized some 3 million fentanyl pills. But even larger quantities went unseized as agents in Albuquerque stood by and watched as drug couriers entered hotels with backpacks believed to be carrying as many as 100,000 fentanyl pills.The entire network could have been dismantled six months earlier, according to a former DEA supervisor who worked on the case and is now among three whistleblowers sounding the alarm about the longstanding practice.The Justice Department's internal watchdog this month announced a nationwide review of government policies and wiretap investigations to determine whether federal authorities have used the same tactic elsewhere."Our investigations are long term and they are complex and they are done under the guidance of the law," DEA Administrator Terry Cole said in an interview this month with Fox News welcoming the inspector general's review. "We will continue to do that, but we need to stay 100% focused on the adversary."___Mustian reported from New York.

Two men were arrested following a nearly monthlong investigation into a string of car burglaries across neighborhoods in Martin County. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office announced the arrests of Stephen Ivan Morris and Shaun Alexander Bilbrey. Both face 36 charges of grand theft, armed burglary, larceny and traveling to commit a burglary. Both were booked into the Martin County Jail on Tuesday. "This probably started with a handful of a few mistakes, and then it escalated rapidly. These kids are in real trouble. They've done a lot of damage in a short period of time, in a one month period of time. For here and now, they've ruined their current life, and they've ruined it for the next couple years as they go through the court system and the prison system, probably," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. See also: Dolly Parton's legacy lives on in Palm Beach County through Imagination Library The investigation into burglaries affecting multiple neighborhoods, including gated communities, began in early August. With assistance from the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office SWAT team and Criminal Investigations Division, Martin County detectives served warrants at the St. Lucie County homes of Morris, 19, and Bilbrey, 19. "None of these were scenarios where they forced their way into the cars. They were simply pulling on door handles and grabbing what was easy to get," Budensiek said. The two men allegedly committed 15 burglaries and stole at least 7 firearms. They also allegedly committed a burglary when they went into an open garage and stole a golf cart and drove it around the neighborhood to commit car burglaries. The car burglaries happened in Hobe Sound, Palm City and two areas in Stuart, including the Stuart Yacht and Country Club. Sheriff Budensiek says the two men may have committed other car burglaries too, that have not been reported yet because the victims are unaware their cars were burglarized. "We have one firearm that was stolen in Hobe Sound, and then traded, according to these young men at a gas station for some cash or some kind of a transaction, and we don't know where that is. If you're the one that has that firearm, we want you to know that it's stolen. You won't be in trouble if you bring it back to us. But if we catch you with it, that'll be a whole different ball game," Budensiek explained. The Sheriff says he has a message for firearm owners. "If you're going to keep a firearm in a car, which is not a good idea to start with, lock your car," he said.

Two people and a dog were evacuated after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames, sending smoke through the garage of their home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the fire started at about 6:30 a.m. Monday near Northeast Cypress Lane in Jensen Beach. When firefighters arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage. The homeowner told crews a lithium-ion battery had been charging inside. MCFR said crews quickly evacuated the home, contained the fire to the garage and extinguished the flames. No other structures were in danger. See also: Amendment 3: What could change in Palm Beach County MCFR is reminding people to unplug batteries when they are finished charging to prevent overheating. CBS12 News has covered numerous fires involving lithium-ion batteries . Most recently, a fire in Fort Pierce began in a shed at a home in May of 2025. Following that fire, officials offered these safety tips: Lithium-ion battery safety tips Only use the charger provided with the device. Avoid extension cords or power strips. Never charge batteries overnight or leave them unattended. Charge and store batteries at room temperature. Keep away from heat, direct sunlight and flammable surfaces. Stop using any battery that is damaged, swollen, leaking or giving off an unusual smell or noise. Charge devices on hard, nonflammable surfaces never on beds, couches or carpets. Disposal reminders: Never throw lithium-ion batteries in the trash or regular recycling. Before recycling, tape the battery terminals with non-conductive tape and place each battery in its own plastic bag. Drop batteries at an approved collection site. Many hardware and office supply stores participate. Check your county or city website for local hazardous waste collection events or drop-off locations. Information on lithium ion batteries can be found on National Fire Prevention Association's website.

Tiger Woods is set to appear in Martin County court Wednesday for a plea conference in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Woods' attorney, Douglas Duncan , filed a notice Tuesday setting the hearing for 8:30 a.m. 2, before Judge Darren Steele at the Martin County Courthouse in Stuart. The filing lists the subject of the hearing as a Change of Plea. The development marks a change from Woods' previous position in the case. In March , the 50-year-old golf legend entered a not guilty plea to misdemeanor charges of DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. It is not yet clear from the newly filed notice what plea Woods intends to enter Wednesday or whether the hearing is part of a negotiated plea agreement. See also: ' Rolling prison’: 2 women accused of heinous sexual abuse, neglect of 4 children The charges stem from a March 27 crash on South Beach Road on Jupiter Island. Investigators said Woods attempted to pass a pickup truck towing a trailer, crossed double solid lines and struck the trailer, causing his Range Rover SUV to roll onto its side. Deputies who responded reported several signs of possible impairment, including bloodshot and glassy eyes, dilated pupils and slow, lethargic movements. They also found two pills later identified as hydrocodone in Woods' pocket, according to the arrest affidavit. Woods told deputies he had been looking down at his phone and adjusting his radio before the crash. A breath test showed no alcohol in his system, but authorities said he refused a urine test. The case has continued through the summer, including a judge's ruling allowing prosecutors access to Woods' medical records related to the case.

A body was found following an extensive search in Martin County, but the sheriff's office could not confirm whether it was that of a man reported missing Aug. On Tuesday, the Martin County Sheriff's Office announced that a body had been recovered from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge. During a news conference, Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Michael Anthony Debevec . In an attempt to return the wallet, the Good Samaritan went to Debevec's home, which ultimately led his family to file a missing person report. Budensiek said investigators later found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. The discovery of the wallet and vehicle prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search. Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to a body. See also: Alligator on I-95 leads to Florida woman being killed in I-95 hit-and-run crash Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed whether the body was Debevec's, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing. "So we do believe we found Mr. Unfortunately, there's a lot of decomposition that's taken place so it's really impossible to determine cause of death. What are we dealing with here? I don't know?" Budensiek said. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found.

One day after trading Quinn Ewers to the Jacksonville Jaguars, the Miami Dolphins landed a new backup quarterback by acquiring Kyle McCord from the Green Bay Packers in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round draft pick.The Dolphins had acquired a 2028 sixth-round selection from Jacksonville in the Ewers trade.McCord had played the Packers’ entire preseason finale against Arizona on Friday and threw four touchdown passes, including two in the final 3 ½ minutes of a 42-38 victory. But the Packers already had a proven backup quarterback on their roster after signing Tyrod Taylor in May.Rather than keeping three quarterbacks on their 53-man roster or trying to see if McCord could clear waivers and land on their practice squad, the Packers sent him to Miami. He becomes the latest recent connection between these two franchises.Miami has former Packers executive Jon-Eric Sullivan as general manager and former Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley as head coach. Now they have acquired McCord from Green Bay to back up Malik Willis, who signed a three-year, $67.5 million contract with Miami in March after backing up Jordan Love in Green Bay for the last two years.The Packers host the Dolphins this season on Dec. 20.McCord spent the 2025 season on the practice squad of the Philadelphia Eagles, who drafted him in the sixth round a year ago. The Packers signed him on Jan. 20.He went 46 of 70 for 446 yards with four touchdowns and no interceptions while getting sacked six times in three preseason games with Green Bay. McCord was 22 of 35 for 226 yards against the Cardinals on Friday."That was the big goal this preseason... to prove that I could play at this level," McCord said after Friday's game. "I feel like the NFL, what we saw tonight, being down two possessions late in the game, being able to come back and make the most out of those drives is huge. Every single game in the NFL comes down to those situations."The 6-foot-3 quarterback played collegiately at Ohio State from 2021-23 and at Syracuse in 2024. He threw for 4,779 yards at Syracuse to set an Atlantic Coast Conference single-season record.

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AP) — Argentina superstar Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international soccer on Monday, ending 21 years of national-team duty that were capped by winning the World Cup in 2022 to secure his place in the pantheon of the game's greatest ever players. “It was a decision that hurt — and still hurts deeply — but I understand that the time has come,” the 39-year-old Messi said on his Instagram account. Messi, who will continue to play at club level with Inter Miami in Major League Soccer, played in a record-tying six World Cups. He won it four years ago in a tournament he dominated in Qatar and also led Argentina to the title match in 2014 and again this year, when the Albiceleste lost to Spain in extra time in New Jersey. Messi stands shoulder to shoulder with Diego Maradona, a compatriot with whom he was so often compared, and Brazil icon Pelé as the greatest players of all time. “I swear to you that I always gave it my all — not just in these last few years when we won everything, but before that too," Messi wrote. "I always fought and left everything on the field for this jersey, to bring you joy and make you feel proud to be Argentine through football.” Messi played 207 games for Argentina and finishes as its all-time leading scorer with 125 goals, 21 of them in World Cups. Only one player has more goals in men's internationals — his long-time rival Cristiano Ronaldo, who has 146 and has yet to announce his retirement from Portugal duty. Messi became the all-time leading World Cup scorer for a month in the recent tournament in the U.S., Mexico and Canada, but finished one goal behind France’s Kylian Mbappé. Messi decided two days after World Cup final In a long social-media post, Messi explained he wrote his retirement letter on July 21 — two days after the World Cup final in which he struggled to make an impact — but waited to publish it because his father was facing health issues that eventually claimed his life. Two months after Messi starred at the 2005 world under-20 championship, scoring both of Argentina's goals in the final triumph, he was given his senior Argentina debut at 18. His first appearance lasted only two minutes; the substitute was sent off against Hungary in Budapest. His journey with the national team was fraught with more frustration — he briefly retired from Argentina duty in 2016 after three defeats in three consecutive major finals — until he finally lifted the World Cup four years ago, either side of also winning Copa America titles in 2021 and '24. “Thank you for all the love these past 20 years," he said. "I’m going to miss hearing you all from the inside so much. Now I’m going to be one of you, cheering and supporting you from the outside (through thick and thin, even more so).” In the letter, Messi did not say how long he intends to continue playing. The recent World Cup showed he's still one of the best players in the world, as did a four-goal display for Inter Miami at the weekend in a 7-1 victory over CF Montreal. “I leave with the peace of mind and pride of having given you — along with my teammates — moments we once only dreamed of. Experiencing this with you was incredible. I love you all,” he added. The second retirement Messi's stellar recent success with Argentina nearly didn’t happen. A decade ago he retired from the national team following Argentina's defeat in the 2016 Copa Amercia final to Chile on penalty kicks — one of which he missed. A public campaign led by Maradona and the president changed his mind and Messi shook off the notion of not being able to win the big matches, returning to the Argentina team and continuing to star for Barcelona, then Paris Saint-Germain, then Inter Miami. He’s the two-time MVP in MLS, the star of the league champion and someone who still creates goals in the biggest moments. He's also a record eight-time world player of the year. “He is pure history,” Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said during the recent World Cup. A legend.” Forever grateful The retirement announcement sparked a wave of reactions. Argentina President Javier Milei wrote on Instagram: “Thank you very much, impossible man.” FIFA President Gianni Infantino praised Messi “for an extraordinary international career that has inspired millions of people and redefined our sport. Your magical talent and humility will be remembered forever.” The Argentine Football Association wrote: “Thank you for everything, Leo. Thank you for representing Argentina. Thank you for making us dream. Thank you for turning so many dreams into reality. The legend is yours, forever.” Argentina and Inter Miami teammate Rodrigo De Paul highlighted on social media “your unconditional love for our country, your internal battles to never give up, your strength in always enduring injustices, and your leadership and character in your dealings with every player.” Leandro Paredes, another Argentina teammate, said, “Thank you for absolutely everything. You are and always will be the greatest of all time. We love you, Captain.” Defender Cristian Romero said: “I love you, I admire you, and I will always be grateful for the impact you’ve had on me and on our country. Thank you for so much, Captain.” ___ AP Sports writers Tim Reynolds and Steve Douglas contributed to this report. ___ See AP’s full soccer coverage here

Residents in Indiantown 's Booker Park neighborhood are cleaning up flooded homes and cars after several inches of rain turned streets into what neighbors described as a lake Saturday. The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory for southwestern Martin County Saturday afternoon after between three and four inches of rain had already fallen, with another one to two inches possible. Photos and video provided to CBS12 News show water covering streets, surrounding homes and reaching vehicles. Other images show water inside a car and residents drying out belongings after the flooding. Booker Park resident, Derek Dowling, spent Monday scooping water out of his flooded car with a kitchen pot. "All the way up to the front seat. Then the whole back seat filled up," Dowling said. "I don't know what else is damaged." Dowling said water also got inside his home and described returning to the neighborhood Saturday to find the street looking "like a swimming pool." Now, he's worried it could happen again. "It makes me nervous that this is going to happen again," Dowling said. For Jean Charles, who lives on Palm Beach Street, the water made its way inside his home too. Charles said the water continued rising even after the rain stopped. He said vehicles driving through the flooded street created waves that pushed even more water toward his house. "When the truck keep pass by, it's boom, boom, boom, boom," Charles said. He said towels placed near the doors weren't enough to stop the water. "It come in the back door and the front door too," Charles said. Charles showed CBS12 News standing water still surrounding parts of his property Monday and pointed to drains he believes aren't working properly. "The drains aren't working," Charles said. He said he had not seen anyone from the Village at his home as of the time we spoke with him Monday. The flooding is raising new questions because Booker Park has already undergone a multimillion-dollar project specifically intended to improve drainage. Village of Indiantown records show officials began a $2.18 million stormwater drainage and roadway improvement project in Booker Park in January 2022. The State of Florida provided $2 million, with another $180,000 coming from the Village. According to the Village, the project was developed after a study examined the neighborhood's existing stormwater system and identified vulnerabilities. Improvements included new swales and driveway culverts specifically designed to alleviate flooding in Booker Park. Village planning documents indicated substantial completion was expected by late 2022. But residents say drainage remains a problem. Charles said some drains were still filled with water Monday, leaving him concerned as rain began falling again. "Water is still can go nowhere," Charles said. Other residents reported similarly severe flooding over the weekend. Some said they were unable to drive out of the neighborhood, while Martin County Sheriff's deputies drove through Booker Park to check on residents. Now residents are left drying carpets, cleaning their homes and assessing damage to vehicles and belongings while questioning what happens when the next heavy storm arrives. CBS12 News has reached out to the Village of Indiantown asking why Booker Park experienced such significant flooding, whether the drainage system performed as designed, what portions of the $2.18 million project were completed and whether additional improvements are planned. We are waiting for the Village's response. Concerned residents may bring this up at a special Village Council meeting Tuesday night at 6 p.m. The special Village Council meeting is Tuesday from 6 to 8 p.m. at the Bob Souza Center, 15565 SW Osceola St. This is a developing story.
