hero.headline: Florida orders removal of license plate cameras from state roads within 30 days
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, citing concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes. The directive includes Flock cameras and comes days after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology out of control and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records.

The decision is drawing mixed reactions from residents. Reid Mollway, a Palm Beach County resident, supports the move. The level of data collection I feel is an invasion of privacy, Mollway said. We're being tracked through data that is not fully clarified and kept for dates that have no expiration. David Vega, another Palm Beach County resident, said the cameras serve an important public safety purpose. I support them being there, Vega said. Vega and others argue the cameras help law enforcement keep communities safer.

The crackdown is also drawing political criticism. Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Local law enforcement agencies have been contacted for comment on how the removal order will affect their operations. Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw responded but did not provide details in the statement.

The 30-day removal deadline means local agencies must dismantle the camera systems from state roads by early October. The order affects cameras installed along highways throughout Florida and represents a significant shift in state policy on automated surveillance technology on public roads.

cards.headline: DeSantis and Byron Donalds to share Tampa stage as Florida Republicans seek unity after primary
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis and Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds are scheduled to appear together at a Republican leadership forum in Tampa on Tuesday, marking an apparent thaw after a contentious primary.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis and Republican gubernatorial nominee Byron Donalds are scheduled to share a stage Tuesday at a Republican leadership forum in Tampa. Attorney General James Uthmeier, Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson are also expected at the event. The appearance follows a primary campaign that exposed a persistent gap between Donalds and the outgoing governor.

DeSantis declined to endorse anyone in the Republican primary, including Lt. Jay Collins, the lieutenant governor he appointed in 2025. DeSantis previously said Donalds had not been part of his administration's victories in Florida. Donalds suggested the friction stemmed from his decision to endorse Donald Trump over DeSantis during the 2024 presidential primary. Donalds won nearly 48 percent of the vote in an 11-candidate field, finishing well ahead of Collins, who took roughly 25 percent.

Tonight, the primary is over, Donalds told supporters on primary night. Tonight, we put aside our differences. Tonight, we are one united Republican Party. Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia predicted the GOP would move past the primary and unite around its statewide slate. I think we're having a Kumbaya moment, Ingoglia said in August. We're all going to get in the same boat, rowing in the same direction. The general election is in November, and Donalds will face Democratic nominee David Jolly in the race to succeed the term-limited DeSantis.

"Tonight, we put aside our differences. Tonight, we are one united Republican Party."The declaration followed a campaign that exposed a persistent gap between Donalds and outgoing Gov. Still, his public criticism of Donalds made the distance between the governor and the eventual nominee especially visible.DeSantis previously said Donalds had not been part of his administration's victories in Florida. Donalds suggested the friction stemmed from his decision to endorse Donald Trump over DeSantis during the 2024 presidential primary. Now comes what looks like a thaw.DeSantis and Donalds are scheduled to share a stage Tuesday at a Republican leadership forum in Tampa. Attorney General James Uthmeier, Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia and Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson are also expected at the event.Florida GOP leaders previously predicted the GOP would move past the primary and unite around its statewide slate."I think we're having a Kumbaya moment," Ingoglia said Aug. "We're all going to get in the same boat, rowing in the same direction."Democrats are attempting their own version of post-primary peace talks, although their unity statement came with an unusually candid caveat.The party's six statewide nominees met Sunday in Miami Lakes and said they were moving forward with "an abundance of goodwill, mutual respect, and friendship." The group included U.S. Senate nominee Angie Nixon; gubernatorial ticket David Jolly and Gwen Graham; attorney general nominee José Javier Rodríguez; CFO nominee Annette Taddeo; and agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins. The Florida Democratic Party previously announced the full slate following the Aug. 18 primary."While we won't be endorsing each other's full platforms, we are fully supporting each other as a ticket to deliver on a more affordable Florida and end corruption in Tallahassee and Washington," the nominees said in their joint statement.They identified housing, healthcare, education and wages as common ground. The reference to their separate platforms, however, underscored the ideological distance between two of the party's most prominent nominees.Nixon pulled off one of primary night's biggest upsets, defeating former national security official Alex Vindman despite being outspent by more than 16 to one. She joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June, although the organization did not endorse her campaign. Nixon has described herself as a social democrat and has tried to center her campaign on working-class economic issues rather than labels.Jolly, a former Republican congressman who later became an independent before joining the Democratic Party, has drawn a clear ideological line. Asked about Nixon after the primary, he said, "I reject socialism. I'm a capitalist and I think capitalism creates the most amount of economic growth." He also acknowledged that the two candidates will disagree on some issues while working together on affordability, healthcare and education. Republicans have already moved to tie Jolly to Nixon's DSA affiliation.Jolly's campaign returned to its unity message Monday, arguing that the election should focus on the cost of living instead of ideological attacks."Punching at other people has never reduced the cost of your insurance, or improved your school, or given you greater access to health care," Jolly said. "Punching at each other just divides us."Both parties have reason to close ranks quickly. Republicans held more than 5.6 million active registrations as of July 31, compared with roughly 4.1 million Democrats, according to the Florida Division of Elections. More than 3.3 million voters were registered without a party affiliation.The general election is Nov. Donalds will face Jolly in the race to succeed the term-limited DeSantis, while Nixon will challenge Republican U.S. Ashley Moody in the special election for the remainder of Marco Rubio's term.For now, both parties have found at least one dependable source of common ground: the other side.

hero.headline: Tiger Woods scheduled for change-of-plea hearing Wednesday in Jupiter Island DUI case
hero.body:
Tiger Woods is scheduled to appear in court Wednesday morning for a change-of-plea hearing in the DUI case stemming from his March rollover crash on Jupiter Island. Court records show the hearing for Eldrick Tiger Woods is set for 8:30 a.m. before Judge Darren Steele in Martin County. The State Attorney's Office confirmed the hearing.

Woods faces two misdemeanor charges following his March 27 arrest: DUI with property damage and refusal to submit to a lawful test. According to court records filed in March, Woods previously submitted a written plea of not guilty and a waiver of arraignment. Court records do not indicate what plea Woods plans to enter or whether the hearing is connected to a negotiated plea agreement.

The charges stem from a rollover crash that occurred shortly before 2 p.m. near Woods' home on South Beach Road. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Woods was driving a Range Rover at a high speed when he approached a pickup truck pulling a pressure-cleaning trailer that was beginning to turn into a driveway. Woods swerved in an attempt to avoid a collision but clipped the back of the trailer, causing his Range Rover to roll onto its side. Woods, who was alone in the SUV, crawled out through the passenger-side door. Neither Woods nor the driver of the pickup truck was injured.

Deputies said Woods showed signs of impairment at the scene and was subsequently arrested. Woods submitted to a breath test and registered no alcohol, according to the sheriff, but refused to provide a urine sample. Investigators said they suspected Woods may have been impaired by medication or another drug rather than alcohol. Because Woods refused the urine test, Budensiek said investigators would not be able to definitively determine what may have caused his alleged impairment. No drugs or medication were found inside Woods' vehicle. Woods was booked into the Martin County Jail and released later that night after posting $1,150 bail. Wednesday's hearing comes nearly a decade after another DUI-related arrest involving Woods in Palm Beach County. In 2017, Woods was arrested on suspicion of DUI and later pleaded guilty to reckless driving as part of a plea deal.

cards.headline: Florida prepares to execute Harold Gene Lucas, first of three executions scheduled this month
cards.teaser: Harold Gene Lucas, 74, is set to receive a lethal injection Tuesday at Florida State Prison near Starke. He would be the 14th prisoner put to death this year in Florida.
cards.body:
Harold Gene Lucas, 74, convicted of fatally shooting a 16-year-old girl who rejected his romantic advances and wounding two of her friends, is set to be executed Tuesday at 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison near Starke. He would be the 14th prisoner put to death this year in Florida. Gov. Ron DeSantis has already signed death warrants for two more executions later this September.

Lucas chose not to file appeals with the Florida Supreme Court or federal courts. He told a circuit judge after his death warrant was issued that he wanted to waive all post-conviction proceedings. Lucas said he has been on death row for 50 years and has no desire to carry this any further, adding that the sooner it's over, the better he'll enjoy it.

Lucas was sentenced to death and resentenced to death four more times after being convicted of first-degree murder and two counts of attempted first-degree murder for the deadly 1976 attack on Jill Piper and the wounding of Richard Byrd Jr. and Terri Rice in Bonita Springs. Two more executions are planned in Florida this month. Daniel Owen Conahan Jr., 72, is scheduled to die on Sept. 10, followed by Curtis Wilkie Beasley, 77, on Sept. 29.
cards.article_text: A Florida man convicted of fatally shooting a 16-year-old girl who rejected his romantic advances and wounding two of her friends is set to be executed Tuesday in the first of three lethal injections scheduled this month in the state.Harold Gene Lucas, 74, is set to receive a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke starting at 6 p.m. He would be the 14th prisoner put to death this year in Florida, and Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has already signed death warrants for two more executions set for later this September.Lucas chose not to file appeals with the Florida Supreme Court or the U.S. He told a circuit judge after his death warrant was issued that he wanted to waive all post-conviction proceedings, and the judge granted his request several days later.“I've been on death row for 50 years, and I have no desire to carry this any further,” Lucas told the judge, according to court transcripts. “The sooner it's over, the better I'll enjoy it. I am tired.”Lucas was sentenced to death — and resentenced to death four more times — after being convicted of first-degree murder and two counts of attempted first-degree murder for the deadly 1976 attack on Jill Piper and the wounding of her friends, Richard Byrd Jr. and Terri Rice.According to court records, Lucas was 24 in August 1976 when he was arrested for trespassing at Piper's Bonita Springs home, south of Fort Myers. Lucas had known the teen for four years and worked for her family, officials said. Lucas and Piper had previously dated, and Lucas told a friend that he planned to marry the girl.About a week after the arrest, Lucas and Piper had two separate confrontations on the same day, several hours apart, investigators said. Witnesses testified that Lucas threatened to kill Piper.Piper asked Byrd and Rice to spend that night at her home for protection, officials said. Lucas eventually showed up with a rifle and shot Piper multiple times while she begged for her life and then shot and wounded her friends, investigators said. Lucas was arrested the next day.Lucas was initially sentenced to death in 1977 with a 12-0 jury recommendation, court records show. The Florida Supreme Court later ruled that the trial judge was wrong to consider the heinousness of the attempted murders while deciding the sentence for the murder. That same trial judge resentenced Lucas to death in 1980.By the time a third sentencing was ordered, the original trial judge had passed away, and a new judge was assigned. That judge sentenced Lucas to death in 1985, but the Florida Supreme Court later ruled that a new jury should hear the case, though the conviction itself would continue to stand. The new jury recommended death by 11-1, and Lucas was sentenced to death for a fourth time in 1987. The Florida Supreme Court ruled the sentencing order wasn't clear, and that second judge sentenced Lucas to death for a fifth and final time in 1990.No appeals after that were successful.A total of 47 people were executed in the U.S. Florida led the way with 19 lethal injections, a record in the state since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida has carried out more than half of the 23 total executions in the U.S. this year.In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Two more executions are planned in Florida later this month. Daniel Owen Conahan Jr., 72, is scheduled to die on Sept. 10, followed by Curtis Wilkie Beasley, 77, on Sept. 29.Conahan was convicted of kidnapping and strangling a man he had paid to pose for nude photos, and authorities suspect him of similar homicides committed in the 1990s in southwest Florida.Beasley was convicted of beating a woman to death with a hammer, robbing her and stealing her car in 1995.All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

hero.headline: Flavor South Florida brings dining deals to Port St. Lucie and Treasure Coast restaurants through September
hero.body:
Flavor South Florida is returning this September with prix fixe dining specials at more than 100 restaurants across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast. The monthlong dining event runs Sept. 1-30 and features lunch, brunch and dinner specials ranging from about $25 to $65 at participating restaurants stretching from Boca Raton to Port St. Lucie.

Kerri Paizzi, CEO of Flavor South Florida, said the annual promotion helps local restaurants during one of the slower tourism periods of the year. September is traditionally the slowest month of the year for restaurant sales because snowbirds aren't quite here yet and we're still kind of in those summer months, Paizzi said. So it's a great local incentive to get people out dining, trying new restaurants, supporting the restaurants and just getting good deals.

This year's event includes more than 100 participating restaurants and dozens of newcomers across South Florida. At PGA National Resort in Palm Beach Gardens, Executive Chef Jeremy Ford of The Butchers Club previewed several dishes featured during Flavor South Florida, including burrata with compressed summer melon and prosciutto, pork belly lettuce wraps and steak frites topped with chimichurri sauce. Ford recently earned a Michelin recommendation for The Butchers Club and said the restaurant is offering a prix fixe menu starting at $65 during the event.

Flavor South Florida organizers released an updated restaurant guide and mobile app to help diners discover and track participating restaurants throughout the month. A complete list of participating restaurants and menus is available at flavorsouthflorida.com.

hero.headline: Indiantown residents face drainage problems after weekend flooding
hero.body:
Indiantown residents confronted new flooding worries Monday as rain returned to the area two days after Saturday's deluge sent water up to front doors and disabled vehicles. Village crews responded Saturday to 6 inches of rain that overwhelmed the drainage system and left residents like Mercy Perry watching water flood his car, which now will not start.

Perry said drainage in Indiantown used to work well before the weekend flooding struck. Village manager Taryn Kryzda said the heavy rainfall in a short period compromised drainage structures even in new development, with no single area escaping problems. Perry saw village crews clearing debris from drains on Saturday.

Kryzda said upgrading the drainage infrastructure will require time and money. The village has already engaged engineers to start the process, she said.

The next steps include creating a capital improvement program to prioritize projects and identifying funding sources, according to Kryzda.

hero.headline: Indiantown's Booker Park floods despite $2.18 million drainage project completed in 2022
hero.body:
Homes and cars flooded in Indiantown's Booker Park neighborhood Saturday after several inches of rain overwhelmed the drainage system, raising questions about a $2.18 million stormwater drainage and roadway improvement project completed in the area. The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory for southwestern Martin County Saturday afternoon after between three and four inches of rain had already fallen, with another one to two inches possible.

Booker Park resident Derek Dowling spent Monday scooping water out of his flooded car with a kitchen pot. Water filled his car all the way up to the front seat and the entire back seat. Water also got inside his home. Jean Charles, who lives on Palm Beach Street, said water came in through both his back door and front door. He said the water continued rising even after the rain stopped, with vehicles driving through the flooded street creating waves that pushed more water toward his house. Charles pointed to drains he believes are not working properly, with standing water still surrounding parts of his property Monday.

Village of Indiantown records show officials began the $2.18 million stormwater drainage and roadway improvement project in Booker Park in January 2022. The State of Florida provided $2 million, with another $180,000 coming from the Village. The project was developed after a study examined the neighborhood's existing stormwater system and identified vulnerabilities. Improvements included new swales and driveway culverts specifically designed to alleviate flooding in Booker Park. Village planning documents indicated substantial completion was expected by late 2022.

Village manager Taryn Kryzda said 6 inches of rain on Saturday simply overwhelmed the drainage system, causing the flooding. Kryzda said drainage structures were compromised even in new development because of so much rain in a short period of time. Upgrading the drainage infrastructure would require engineering work already underway, followed by creating a capital improvement program to prioritize projects and identifying funding sources. Resident Mercy Perry said he saw village crews out clearing debris from drains on Saturday. Some residents reported they were unable to drive out of the neighborhood, while Martin County Sheriff's deputies drove through Booker Park to check on residents.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners receiving notices about Waste Pro settlement credits on tax bills
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with its former trash hauler will show up on their property tax bills. The credits are the result of the city's lawsuit against Waste Pro, the company Port St. Lucie sued after two years of unreliable service and missed pickups. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The settlement is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties with a significant difference in amounts. About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll would receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, would receive an estimated $64 credit.

In June, the City Council voted to return all of that money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision drew loud objections at the June meeting. Residents told the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

The credits are landing at the same time property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it is the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. FCC Environmental Services is the city's current trash hauler. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

hero.headline: Indiantown's Booker Park floods despite $2.18 million drainage project completed in 2022
hero.body:
Residents in Indiantown's Booker Park neighborhood are cleaning up flooded homes and cars after several inches of rain turned streets into what neighbors described as a lake Saturday, raising questions about a $2.18 million stormwater drainage project completed to prevent such flooding. The National Weather Service issued a flood advisory for southwestern Martin County Saturday afternoon after between three and four inches of rain had already fallen, with another one to two inches possible.

Village of Indiantown records show officials began a $2.18 million stormwater drainage and roadway improvement project in Booker Park in January 2022. The State of Florida provided $2 million, with another $180,000 coming from the Village. According to the Village, the project was developed after a study examined the neighborhood's existing stormwater system and identified vulnerabilities. Improvements included new swales and driveway culverts specifically designed to alleviate flooding in Booker Park, with substantial completion expected by late 2022.

Derek Dowling spent Monday scooping water out of his flooded car with a kitchen pot. Water reached the front and back seats of his vehicle and got inside his home. Dowling described returning to the neighborhood Saturday to find the street looking like a swimming pool. For Jean Charles, who lives on Palm Beach Street, the water made its way inside his home too. Charles said the water continued rising even after the rain stopped, with vehicles driving through the flooded street creating waves that pushed more water toward his house. Charles showed standing water still surrounding parts of his property Monday and pointed to drains he believes are not working properly.

Village manager Taryn Kryzda said 6 inches of rain on Saturday simply overwhelmed the drainage system, causing the flooding. Kryzda said crews found that even in new development, drainage structures were compromised because of so much rain in a short period of time. Upgrading the drainage infrastructure would require engineering work already underway, creation of a capital improvement program to prioritize projects, and identification of funding. Residents reported some were unable to drive out of the neighborhood, while Martin County Sheriff's deputies drove through Booker Park to check on residents.

cards.headline: Charging lithium-ion battery sparks Jensen Beach garage fire, two people and dog evacuated
cards.teaser: Martin County Fire Rescue responded to a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames.
cards.body:
Two people and a dog were evacuated after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames, sending smoke through the garage of their home. Martin County Fire Rescue said the fire started at about 6:30 a.m. Monday near Northeast Cypress Lane in Jensen Beach. When firefighters arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage. The homeowner told crews a lithium-ion battery had been charging inside.

MCFR said crews quickly evacuated the home, contained the fire to the garage and extinguished the flames. No other structures were in danger. MCFR is reminding people to unplug batteries when they are finished charging to prevent overheating. Officials recommend only using the charger provided with the device, avoiding extension cords or power strips, and never charging batteries overnight or leaving them unattended. Batteries should be charged and stored at room temperature and kept away from heat, direct sunlight and flammable surfaces.

The homeowner told crews a lithium-ion battery had been charging inside. MCFR said crews quickly evacuated the home, contained the fire to the garage and extinguished the flames. CBS12 News has covered numerous fires involving lithium-ion batteries . Most recently, a fire in Fort Pierce began in a shed at a home in May of 2025. Following that fire, officials offered these safety tips: Lithium-ion battery safety tips Only use the charger provided with the device. Avoid extension cords or power strips. Never charge batteries overnight or leave them unattended. Charge and store batteries at room temperature. Keep away from heat, direct sunlight and flammable surfaces. Stop using any battery that is damaged, swollen, leaking or giving off an unusual smell or noise. Charge devices on hard, nonflammable surfaces never on beds, couches or carpets. Disposal reminders: Never throw lithium-ion batteries in the trash or regular recycling. Before recycling, tape the battery terminals with non-conductive tape and place each battery in its own plastic bag. Drop batteries at an approved collection site. Many hardware and office supply stores participate. Check your county or city website for local hazardous waste collection events or drop-off locations. Information on lithium ion batteries can be found on National Fire Prevention Association's website.

hero.headline: Florida Department of Transportation revokes permits for automated license plate readers statewide
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation revoked all statewide permits for automated license plate recognition systems on Monday, blocking future requests from local law enforcement agencies. Will Watts, the chief operating officer and assistant secretary for FDOT, issued a memo to all permit holders statewide announcing the department had revoked all LPR-related approvals it issued to local law enforcement agencies. The department cited privacy concerns, reports of misuse and what it calls surveillance schemes as reasons for the decision.

The revocation does not eliminate every license plate reader in Florida, only those installed by local agencies along state-controlled roads. The action follows Governor Ron DeSantis seeking an overview of license plate camera reader use across the state. FDOT is now blocking all future requests from local agencies to install the technology on state roads.

Also on Monday, the Leon County Sheriff's Office suspended its use of automated license plate recognition technology while awaiting stronger oversight measures, Sheriff Walt McNeil announced. The timing of the sheriff's office suspension coincided with the state transportation department's statewide permit revocation.

Automated license plate recognition systems use cameras to capture and store images of vehicle license plates, typically to track vehicle movements or identify stolen vehicles and wanted suspects. The technology has drawn criticism from privacy advocates who argue the systems enable mass surveillance of law-abiding citizens. The FDOT memo marks a significant shift in policy for the state agency, which had previously approved local law enforcement requests to install the readers along state-maintained roadways throughout Florida.

hero.headline: Indiantown begins drainage infrastructure review after Saturday flooding
hero.body:
Indiantown village officials have engaged engineers to review drainage infrastructure after 6 inches of rain on Saturday overwhelmed the system and flooded neighborhoods. Village manager Taryn Kryzda said the rainfall caused flooding across multiple areas, including new developments where drainage structures were compromised.

Resident Mercy Perry said water came up to his front door and flooded his car, which no longer starts. Perry said the village used to have fairly good drainage and residents never experienced flooding like Saturday's before. Perry said he saw village crews clearing debris from drains on Saturday.

Kryzda said upgrading the drainage infrastructure will require engineering work, capital improvement planning, and funding. The village manager said engineers will first assess the system, then officials will create a capital improvement program to prioritize projects and identify funding sources.

More rain fell in Indiantown on Monday, raising concerns among residents still dealing with Saturday's flooding damage. Kryzda said the flooding was not confined to one specific area and affected even newer developments in the village.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners receiving notices about Waste Pro settlement credits on property tax bills
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie homeowners are finding flyers in their mailboxes explaining how the city's $24 million settlement with Waste Pro will appear as credits on their property tax bills. The settlement money is being distributed over 95,000 eligible properties following the city's lawsuit against its former trash hauler for two years of unreliable service and missed pickups.

About 57,000 homeowners who have stayed at the same property since the 2022 tax roll will receive an estimated $364 credit. Roughly 38,000 other eligible properties, including newer properties added to the tax roll and those approved through an eligibility claims process, will receive an estimated $64 credit. The two sides settled in April for $24 million, days before the case was set to go to trial.

The City Council voted in June to return all of the settlement money to residents through property tax credits rather than mailing checks. The decision drew loud objections at the June meeting, with residents telling the council they wanted cash in hand. Only Councilwoman Jolien Caraballo supported that approach. Other council members raised concerns about the cost of printing and mailing tens of thousands of checks and the chance that payments could be lost or stolen. When the final vote was taken, boos and jeers came from the audience.

The credits are landing as property owners across St. Lucie County are receiving their TRIM notices, the annual estimate of what they can expect to owe in property taxes. Council members agreed that none of the settlement money would be moved into the city's general fund. Councilman Anthony Bonna said it's the taxpayers' money and the taxpayers were the ones who were wronged. Port St. Lucie's current trash hauler is FCC Environmental Services. Voters are expected to weigh in on twice-weekly pickup through a straw ballot question in November.

hero.headline: Former Treasure Coast Hospice employee arrested for stealing rings from dead patient in Stuart
hero.body:
A former Treasure Coast Hospice employee was arrested after Stuart police say she stole two rings from a deceased patient and pawned one of them in Port St. Lucie. Latoya Morrine Moye of Fort Pierce faces a third-degree grand theft charge in connection with the theft.

Stuart Police Department officers received a report on Aug. 18 that two rings were missing from a deceased Treasure Coast Hospice patient. A detective searched pawn transaction records and discovered that Moye had pawned a ring in Port St. Lucie one day after it was reported missing. The ring was recovered, and the patient's family identified it as one of the two missing rings.

Pawn records and surveillance video identified Moye as the person who made the transaction, according to Stuart police. A warrant was issued for her arrest, and she was later arrested in St. Lucie County.

The second ring remains missing. Treasure Coast Hospice is covering the cost of retrieving the recovered ring and returning it to the family.

hero.headline: Two people, dog escape Jensen Beach garage fire caused by charging lithium-ion battery
hero.body:
Two people and a dog safely escaped a garage fire Monday morning in Jensen Beach after a charging lithium-ion battery burst into flames, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The fire was reported just after 6:30 a.m. in the 2700 block of Northeast Cypress Lane. When crews arrived, they found heavy smoke coming from the garage of the home.

The homeowner told firefighters they had been charging a lithium-ion battery in the garage when the fire started. Martin County Fire Rescue and Stuart Fire Rescue crews immediately evacuated the residence and worked to contain the flames. Firefighters extinguished the fire before it could spread to other structures, and no neighboring properties were threatened.

Fire rescue officials called the incident a close call and are reminding residents to follow proper lithium-ion battery safety practices. They encourage people to unplug batteries once they are fully charged to help prevent overheating and potential fires. Officials recommend charging devices on hard, nonflammable surfaces and never leaving batteries charging overnight or unattended.

Lithium-ion batteries are commonly found in smartphones, laptops, e-bikes, scooters, and many other electronic devices. While generally safe when used properly, they can pose fire risks if damaged, overcharged, or exposed to extreme temperatures. Residents should stop using any battery that is damaged, swollen, leaking or giving off an unusual smell or noise. Additional safety guidelines are available on the National Fire Protection Association's website.

According to the homeowner, a lithium-ion battery had been charging in the garage before the fire started. hero.headline: Flooding traps dozens of Indiantown residents in Booker Park neighborhood, sparks drainage system concerns
hero.body:
Dozens of residents in Indiantown's Booker Park neighborhood were trapped in their homes Saturday when floodwaters from heavy rain swamped streets and made it impossible to drive in or out of the area. Angela Harrell, who has lived in Indiantown for more than 20 years, said she has never seen flooding this severe and had to park her car two streets over.

Resident Melody Baum said the problem extends beyond the rainfall itself to a failure in the neighborhood's drainage infrastructure. The drain is lower than what the water takes in, causing water to back up rather than drain away. Baum said the flooding is so severe it is pushing water into a nearby home.

Baum warned neighbors about potential dangers in the floodwater, saying catfish and ducks were visible in the water and she would not be surprised if a water moccasin was nearby. She also expressed concern about bacteria in the floodwater. Martin County Sheriff's deputies drove through the area to check on residents.

Harrell said the situation raises concerns about what a more serious storm could bring, noting this was not a tropical storm or hurricane. Baum is asking neighbors to stay inside until the water drains and is calling for a solution to the drainage system in the community.

hero.headline: Martin County Sheriff's Office searches for Oklahoma visitor last seen at Hutchinson Island beach
hero.body:
The Martin County Sheriff's Office is attempting to locate a missing man visiting the area from Oklahoma. Michael Debevec was last seen Wednesday afternoon at Chastain Beach, known as "The Rocks," on the southern tip of Hutchinson Island, where his vehicle was found. His family has not heard from him, and he may be experiencing an emotional breakdown, the agency said.

Debevec's LinkedIn page lists him as from Broken Arrow, Oklahoma. He is 5-foot-7 with blue eyes. The Sheriff's Office did not disclose his age. The agency posted the information on Facebook seeking public assistance in locating him.

hero.headline: Iron Knight Gym in Port St. Lucie hosts Treasure Coast Hyrox Trials with over 70 athletes this weekend
hero.body:
Over 70 athletes are competing this weekend in the Treasure Coast Hyrox Trials, a local fitness competition hosted by Iron Knight Gym in Port St. Lucie. The gym opened in 2017 and has grown over the past nine years as a facility dedicated to powerlifting and the community built around it.

Nikki Baker, the gym's general manager, said the sport is about more than moving heavy weight. Baker said athletes and coaches push themselves and a whole lot of weight in pursuit of something deeper than physical strength. Baker said the philosophy is personal for her, noting that physical strength helped her understand her mental strength as well.

Baker said growth at Iron Knight is measured not just in weight lifted, but in personal progress. She described it as being better than you were a week ago or a day ago, and overcoming things that you literally walked in and said you could not do. Beyond the physical and mental gains, Baker said building community is central to what the gym does.

Baker said the gym knows what your name is, what your dog's name is, and what your goals are. In addition to powerlifting, Iron Knight Gym offers group classes, online coaching, and personal training. Baker said Iron Knight welcomes everyone from beginners to professionals.

hero.headline: Man injured when lightning strikes boat near Sandsprit Park in Stuart
hero.body:
A man was injured Saturday afternoon when lightning struck a boat near Sandsprit Park in Stuart, according to Martin County Fire Rescue and the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Martin County Fire Rescue units and sheriff's deputies responded just before 1 p.m. Saturday to the 3400 block of Southeast St. Lucie Boulevard.

Three people were aboard the boat trolling about 6 miles offshore when lightning struck the outrigger and disintegrated the rod. One man told paramedics he felt the lightning strike hit his head. He was conscious and alert when paramedics transported him to the hospital by ground with minor injuries.

The other two passengers aboard reported minor injuries and refused transport. The lightning strike destroyed the fishing rod on the outrigger when it hit the boat offshore from the Stuart waterfront park.

Martin County Fire Rescue transported the injured man to a local hospital for treatment of minor injuries sustained in the offshore lightning strike Saturday afternoon.

hero.headline: Three arrested in St. Lucie County convenience store drug bust after detectives find crack cocaine, marijuana
hero.body:
Three St. Lucie County men were arrested Friday after detectives executed a search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store located at 1502 Avenue D and recovered crack cocaine and marijuana packaged for sale, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Detectives with the agency's Special Investigations Division secured several people at the business before conducting a search of the property. During the search, investigators found about 14 grams of crack cocaine and 128 grams of marijuana packaged for sale.

Authorities arrested Ayhem Jaber Ubayda, 21, and John Alvin J. Mobley, 71, each charged with possession of marijuana with intent to sell within 1,000 feet of a convenience store. Melvin James Kelly, 60, was charged with possession of cocaine and had an outstanding warrant for sale of cocaine.

The arrests followed the execution of a narcotics search warrant at the Avenue D location. The Special Investigations Division conducted the operation that led to the three men being taken into custody.

hero.headline: One hospitalized after apartment fire at Peacock Run complex in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
One person was taken to a local hospital in stable condition after a structure fire Saturday in an apartment at Peacock Run Apartments in Port St. Lucie, the St. Lucie County Fire District said. SLCFD crews responded to the reported structure fire after reports of smoke and flames coming from a first-floor apartment. The complex is off Interstate 95.

Occupants were evacuating the building before firefighters arrived. The SLCFD crew found moderate smoke coming from the porch area of a first-floor apartment in the three-story building. The crew initiated a fire attack, followed by searches of the affected apartment and building to ensure occupants were safely evacuated.

Firefighters located two pets inside the apartment. One cat was successfully treated with oxygen and recovered. A bird was removed from the apartment but did not survive.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation. The American Red Cross was contacted to assist affected occupants. After the emergency was under control, firefighters took time with some of the children who had evacuated, teaching them about water supply and handing out fire helmets.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies use multiple drones to capture hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in Palm City swamp
hero.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in a swamp during a two-hour manhunt earlier this week. The drones helped deputies track Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, who was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash near the Windstone community in Palm City.

Major Ruben Romero said the drones were the first to get a visual on the suspect, who was hiding underwater. Daceus dipped down, came up to take a breath, and then went right back down into the swampy water. At least seven drone operators tracked the suspect's movements and shared information with Sheriff John Budensiek, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt.

Drone footage shows deputies searching the swampy area with alligators and snakes present. Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as drone operators guided them through the terrain. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt.

Daceus was taken into custody after the two-hour search. Romero said the suspect tried to swim and get away from the drones but could not. Daceus faces several charges. Romero said drones are a tool that has helped law enforcement in recent times and keeps deputies and the community safe.

cards.headline: Hit-and-run suspect arrested after quarter-mile manhunt through Palm City natural lands
cards.teaser: Likenson Daceus led Martin County deputies through dense woods and swamp before being arrested a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands. The manhunt began at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road after a head-on crash.
cards.body:
Likenson Daceus led deputies through dense woods and swamp before being arrested a quarter mile into Palm City natural lands following a hit-and-run crash at SW Rivers End Way and Murphy Road. A deputy spotted the suspect's car in Palm City and attempted a traffic stop, but the suspect fled. Daceus then crashed head-on into another vehicle, leaving the driver with minor injuries. The police report says he left a juvenile in his car before taking off on foot.

The manhunt involved multiple agencies including Martin County Sheriff's Office, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, and Port St. Lucie Police. They utilized road patrols, K-9 teams, aviation and drone units. Sheriff John Budensiek said deputies tracked Daceus through the neighborhood, through several yards, through dense woods, through a backyard, and then into the swamp. Deputies found his hat and picked up a track.

Two hours after the search began, Daceus was in handcuffs. He is charged with one felony and a misdemeanor for fleeing with disregard for safety and resisting arrest. Tanya Talanczuck, a resident near the Windstone community, said she sheltered in place during the search and was relieved by the outcome.

hero.headline: Vero Beach utility bills to jump 47% by 2029 as city approves four-year rate increase
hero.body:
Vero Beach utility customers will pay nearly $39 more each month by 2029 after the City Council and Utility Commission unanimously approved a four-year rate increase plan to fund a $217 million capital improvement program. A typical residential customer using 4,000 gallons per month currently pays $83.54 for combined water and sewer service. By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly, a 46.7% increase over current rates.

The rate increases stem from construction of a new Water Reclamation Facility in Vero Beach and related infrastructure improvements planned through 2030. The city will issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027 to finance the project, structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate. An additional $42.3 million in grants will support the project. The bond amount grew from an $80 million projection in a 2022 rate study to $125 million due to cost escalation.

Water rates will increase 10% in fiscal year 2027, 7.5% in fiscal year 2028, and 5% in each of the following two years. Wastewater rates face steeper increases of 15% in both fiscal years 2027 and 2028, 10% in 2029, and 5% in 2030. Reclaimed water customers will see 25% increases in both 2027 and 2028, followed by 5% annual increases. The utility's operating expenses will grow from approximately $25.6 million in fiscal year 2026 to more than $32 million by 2030.

The ordinance creates a new Wastewater Readiness-to-Serve Charge of $40.85 monthly for property owners who receive city water service but use septic tanks while having public wastewater service available nearby. The charge rises to $54.24 monthly by October 2029. Property owners receive 75 days notice before the charge takes effect. New rates take effect October 1, with subsequent annual adjustments each October. Once the 2027 increases take effect, Vero Beach's $107.30 bill will exceed Fort Pierce Utilities Authority's $95.76 and Indian River County Sewer's $67.70 for the same 4,000-gallon usage level.

By 2029, that same bill will reach $122.45 monthly — an increase of nearly $39 per month, or 46.7% over current rates. The centerpiece is a new Water Reclamation Facility currently under construction in Vero Beach. To finance the project, the city plans to issue $125 million in revenue bonds in February 2027. The bonds are structured over 30 years at a 4.55% interest rate, creating average annual debt service of approximately $8.66 million. An additional $42.3 million in grants will also support the project. The bond amount represents a significant jump from earlier projections. hero.headline: Three arrested after drug search at St. Lucie County convenience store yields crack cocaine, marijuana
hero.body:
Three men were arrested Friday after St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office detectives executed a narcotics search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store located at 1502 Avenue D and recovered crack cocaine and marijuana packaged for sale. Detectives with the agency's Special Investigations Division secured several people at the business before conducting a search of the property.

During the search, investigators found about 14 grams of crack cocaine and 128 grams of marijuana packaged for sale. The drugs were located at the convenience store during the operation.

Authorities arrested Ayhem Jaber Ubayda, 21, and charged him with possession of marijuana with intent to sell within 1,000 feet of a convenience store. Mobley, 71, was charged with possession of marijuana with intent to sell within 1,000 feet of a convenience store. Melvin James Kelly, 60, was charged with possession of cocaine and an outstanding warrant for the sale of cocaine.

The investigation was conducted by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Special Investigations Division. All three suspects were taken into custody at the scene Friday.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie homeowners to receive credits on solid waste bills from $24 million Waste Pro settlement
hero.body:
Thousands of homeowners in Port St. Lucie will receive credits applied to their solid waste bills this year following a $24 million settlement the city received from its former trash hauler, Waste Pro, after a legal dispute related to its prior solid waste collection contract. The city has begun mailing flyers to residents explaining the credits, which will be applied to the 2026-2027 tax bill.

Homeowners who have lived in Port St. Lucie since 2022 will receive the maximum credit of $364. That brings this year's total waste assessment from around $482 down to $118 for those residents. Newer residents will receive a $64 credit. Homeowners who had title changes since 2022 and can prove continuous ownership will receive the $64 credit and may be eligible for an additional $300 at a later time.

Scott Samples with the city said the full settlement amount is being returned to residents. The city council is committed to giving all of the money back from that $24 million, Samples said. He explained that the credits recognize those most directly impacted as residential property owners, and that even newer residents were still paying a higher price than they would have if the contract had been honored.

Resident Steven Lombardi received the maximum credit of $364 and said he is cautiously optimistic. Lombardi said the savings are welcome, but he wishes the city had considered another use for the settlement money, such as extra pickups for twice-weekly trash collection. Two-day trash pickup is up to voters through a straw ballot question this November in Port St. Lucie. It is non-binding, meaning it will serve as a recommendation for council to approve.

hero.headline: Palm City boaters raise concerns about parking space sizes at Charlie Leighton Park after $4.5 million renovation
hero.teaser: Some boaters say the new parking spaces at Charlie Leighton Park's boat ramp are too small for trucks towing larger boats after a $4.5 million overhaul that redid the ramp, added docks, and expanded parking.
hero.body:
Some boaters in Palm City are raising concerns about whether they will still be able to use Charlie Leighton Park's boat ramp after a $4.5 million overhaul. Nick Yahn, a resident who has used the park to launch his boat, measured the new parking spaces and found his truck and trailer would no longer fit. He said the vehicle would be sticking out into the road. Fellow boater Casey Wallace said anything over 20-something feet will not be able to park at the facility.

The park has been under construction since last September. Martin County redid the boat ramp and dredged the adjacent area, installed floating docks, added greenspace and gazebos, built two piers, and expanded the number of parking spaces. The total project cost approximately $4.5 million. Roughly $1.2 million went toward water-related improvements, partially funded by a state grant. The remaining portion covered the rest of the park and parking lot.

Jessica Ballash, deputy director of Martin County Parks and Recreation, explained that typical boat ramp parking space sizes range from 40 to 50 feet and the new spaces are 45 feet. The county said there were previously only 20 designated boat parking spaces and there are now six more. Ballash said the design prioritized safety and organization, as people previously parked wherever they could fit. The county suggested boaters who need longer trailer parking use other county boat ramps, including Jensen Beach and Sandsprit Park. The boat ramp is scheduled to officially open in late September.

cards.headline: Martin County deputies use multiple drones to capture hit-and-run suspect hiding underwater in Palm City swamp
cards.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies used multiple drones to locate and apprehend a hit-and-run suspect who was hiding underwater in a swamp near the Windstone community in Palm City earlier this week. The suspect, identified as Likenson Daceus of Fort Pierce, was wanted for leaving the scene of a hit-and-run crash. Deputies conducted a manhunt that lasted approximately two hours.

The drones provided the first visual confirmation of Daceus, who was hiding underwater in the swampy area. Major Ruben Romero said the suspect would dip down into the water, come up to take a breath, and then go back down. At least seven drone operators tracked the suspect's movements and shared information with the sheriff, who was on the ground and actively involved in the manhunt. Body camera footage shows deputies wading through water as drone operators guided them to the suspect's location.

Major Romero said drones have become a valuable tool for law enforcement in navigating difficult terrain. He noted that deputies saw alligators and snakes in the area during the search. The drones helped keep both deputies and the community safe during the operation. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and Port St. Lucie Police also took part in the manhunt.

Daceus was taken into custody and faces several charges. Major Romero said the suspect tried to swim and get away from the drones but could not escape their tracking capability. The sheriff was seen in dramatic video footage chopping through the swamp while searching for the suspect. Deputies may not have had the suspect in their line of sight at all times, but the drones maintained constant visual contact throughout the manhunt.

hero.headline: Florida rejects $18 billion Meta settlement, becomes sole state to pursue independent lawsuit over youth safety
hero.body:
Florida has become the only state in the nation to reject its share of a nearly $18 billion settlement with Meta over allegations the company knowingly harmed children's mental health with addictive platforms. Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the state will proceed with its own lawsuit against the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, calling the national settlement insufficient and a slap on the wrist for the trillion-dollar corporation.

The 48-state agreement requires Meta to pay nearly $18 billion over 10 years to participating states and territories for youth online safety programs. Uthmeier described the payouts as peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta's profit-driven addictive features inflicted on children. He argued the total settlement amounts to roughly one month of revenue for Meta and fails to create a real deterrent.

The settlement mandates new safety features on Meta's platforms, including a two-hour daily time limit for teenage users, blocking platform access between midnight and 6 a.m., and muting all notifications during school hours. Meta has committed to paying 70% of the settlement upfront, with the remaining 30% contingent on competitors like YouTube and TikTok agreeing to similar restrictions. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson said Meta told parents everywhere that their top concern was the safety of their children when it was actually making money.

Florida's independent case against Meta is just beginning. Uthmeier has pledged that Florida will hold Meta accountable, stating that corporations like Meta will never learn a lesson if they do not incur real costs for breaking the law.

Scott Samples with the city said the full settlement amount is being returned to residents. The city council is committed to giving all of the money back from that $24 million, Samples said. Resident Steven Lombardi received the maximum credit of $364 and said he is cautiously optimistic, adding he will believe it when the credit comes.

Lombardi said the savings are welcome, but he wishes the city had considered another use for the settlement money, suggesting the city could have used the funds to provide extra pickups. Two-day trash pickup is up to voters through a straw ballot question this November in Port St. Lucie. The ballot question is non-binding, meaning it will serve as a recommendation for council to approve.

cards.headline: Three St. Lucie County men arrested after narcotics search at convenience store
cards.teaser: Three individuals were arrested on Friday following a search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store in St. Lucie County, where detectives recovered crack cocaine and marijuana packaged for sale.
cards.body:
Ayhem Jaber Ubayda, 21, John Alvin J. Mobley, 71, and Melvin James Kelly, 60, were each arrested on Friday following a search warrant at Sams Drive Thru convenience store located at 1502 Avenue Drive, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriffs Office. During the search, detectives recovered around 14 grams of crack cocaine and 128 grams of marijuana packaged for sale.

Ubayda and Mobley were each charged with Possession of Marijuana with Intent to Sell within 1,000 Feet of a Convenience Store. Kelly was charged with Possession of Cocaine, and had an outstanding warrant for Sale of Cocaine.

lead_independence.headline: Fort Pierce legal department shakeup raises questions over development decisions
lead_independence.lead: The City Commission decided not to renew City Attorney Sara Hedges' contract. At the same time, Assistant City Attorney Felicia Holloman has resigned, and temporary attorney Caroline Valentin is set to leave at the end of the month, leaving the city searching for new legal leadership. This week, commissioners voted 3-2 to move forward with appointing Deputy City Manager Camille Wallace as interim city attorney while a search is conducted for a permanent replacement.
